articles.title: A man who spent decades on Utah's death row is released and awaits a new trial in a 1985 killing
articles.summary: A 71-year-old man who was convicted of killing a police chief's aunt and spent decades on death row was released Monday after prosecutors said newly analyzed...
articles.body:
A 71-year-old man who was convicted of killing a police chief's aunt and spent decades on death row was released Monday after prosecutors said newly analyzed DNA evidence doesn't link him to the crime.

A Utah judge ordered Douglas Stewart Carter let out on bail late Monday over objections from the victim's family. Carter is required to wear a GPS monitor while he awaits a new trial in the 1985 killing of Eva Olesen.

The state Supreme Court ordered a new trial last year, citing misconduct by investigators. Carter has maintained his innocence and says a signed confession was coerced.

No physical evidence linked him to the crime scene. But the jury convicted Carter, a Black man, based on the confession and the testimony of two witnesses who said he bragged about killing Olesen, who was white. Those witnesses later recanted.

A DNA analysis received Sept. 22 excluded Carter as a possible match to blood found on a doorknob and genetic material recovered from the handle of a knife used to stab Olesen, who was also shot.

Judge Derek Pullan said those results further undermined the case against Carter, but a reasonable jury still could conclude that he killed Olesen.

Carter was released late Monday and ordered not to have any contact with Olesen's family.

"If the state of Utah had their way, he would have been executed 15, 20 years ago before we discovered the misconduct," defense attorney Neal Hamilton said after learning of the judge's order. He urged prosecutors to seek dismissal of an aggravated murder charge still pending against Carter.

Carter will be placed in an extended stay hotel near the family of his son, Tyler Anger, who was adopted by another family as an infant and didn't learn about the conviction until years later, Hamilton said. Carter also will need therapy to deal with his extended incarceration, the attorney said.

"This is going to be a lot for him," Anger said as he waited outside the Utah County jail, where Carter was held. "I want Doug to put his feet on the grass. He hasn't done that in 40 years."

A two-month retrial was planned next year, but last week county prosecutors withdrew a notice that they intended to seek the death penalty.

Utah County prosecutor Erwin Petilos told the judge Monday that reassessing Carter's bail was "necessary and fair" as the state continues to look at the remaining evidence in the case.

Carter, a Chicago native, was living with his mother in Utah when Olesen was killed on Feb. 27, 1985. Court documents indicate the investigation eventually focused on Carter, who was suspected of killing Olesen during a robbery.

By that April, Carter had fled Utah believing he was a suspect in an unrelated assault case, according to court documents. He was apprehended that June in Nashville, Tennessee, where he signed a confession while under interrogation by a Provo detective.

Carter said later that he falsely confessed after police repeatedly threatened him. He was convicted and sentenced to death after a trial in which the defense called no witnesses. He was again sentenced to death after a 1992 retrial, and courts in Utah rejected numerous appeals from Carter in subsequent years.

Key witnesses say police gave them cash and gifts

A turning point came in 2011, when the two witnesses from Carter's original trial were tracked down in Mexico. They said they had been told to lie in court and had received cash and gifts from police, who told them not to disclose the payments. They also said police and prosecutors threatened them and their son with deportation if they did not implicate Carter.

More than a decade of legal wrangling followed before the Utah Supreme Court last year ordered a new trial, citing "multiple instances of intentional misconduct" by police and a prosecutor. A DNA analysis of the evidence was conducted in response to that order, and prosecutors said the results arrived last week. They declined Monday to say whether they're using the DNA evidence to search for other suspects with matching DNA.

Carter's defense attorneys have said witnesses saw a white man fleeing the crime scene and an investigator suppressed evidence pointing to other suspects, including the victim's husband, Orla Olesen.

They allege that prosecutors were close to filing charges against the husband, but a Provo police lieutenant asked them not to so he could continue investigating. Carter was identified as a suspect soon after, according to court documents.

Orla Olesen, a painting contractor who died in 2009, told police he found his wife dead in their home, partially undressed and with her hands tied behind her back.

Theresa Olesen, a daughter-in-law of Eva Olesen, said during Monday's bond hearing that her family had "serious concerns" about Carter's release.

"By golly we were hoping for a concrete match," Olesen said of the DNA analysis. "It doesn't mean he wasn't there."

"We just want justice for Eva. And if he had any part of it we want that to be known," she added. ___ Associated Press photographer George Frey in Provo, Utah, contributed to this report.

articles.title: UK weather: Temperatures to hit 25C in burst of late September warmth
articles.summary: Temperatures are expected to rise well above the late September average on Tuesday with a very warm night to follow, as Simon King explains.
articles.body:
Temperatures could reach as high as 25C in parts of the UK on Tuesday in a burst of late September warmth.

The warmest locations will be across the south-east of England, though temperatures will widely reach into the 20s Celsius across England and the high teens elsewhere.

This will be around 3 to 6 degrees above the average for the time of year.

Tuesday night will also be unusually warm with the temperature in some locations not falling much below 20C.

The boost in temperatures will come as a strong southerly airflow develops into Tuesday.

With unusually hot air across France and Spain - where temperatures have widely been in excess of 30C - the southerly wind will bring some of this warmth to the UK.

Temperatures across England will exceed 20C widely with the highest temperatures in south-east England where it will get into the mid-20s Celsius.

Average temperatures across England in late September are around 16 to 19C.

While there could be a lot of cloud with a few showers on Tuesday morning, sunny spells will develop over England and Wales.

It will also be warmer than average across Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland with maximum temperatures on Tuesday of 17 to 22C.

However, after starting sunny here, cloud will increase during the day.

The southerly winds will strengthen with gusts up to 50mph expected in Northern Ireland and western Scotland.

This is linked to a large and deep area of low pressure moving north in the eastern Atlantic toward Iceland.

Nighttime temperatures may not fall below 20C

The warm southerly winds will continue overnight into Wednesday with minimum temperatures more typical of a summer's night than early autumn.

In parts of south-east England, it is not out of the question that temperatures won't dip below 20C overnight.

Overnight temperatures in late September are typically around 7 to 11C, so this will make for an unusually warm night.

September will mark another month where average temperatures will come in well above normal.

Up to 26 September, the Central England Temperature (CET) - the world's longest running temperature record, which tracks the average temperature across various locations in England - is 2.6 degrees Celsius above normal.

Every month this calendar year has seen the average mean CET above average. It is also 2.6C higher than normal for the year to date.

It would need to be much colder than normal during the rest of the year for 2026 to not be one the warmest on record for the UK.

The Met Office's latest three-month outlook, spanning October to December, suggests higher-than-normal chances of a mild autumn and start to winter.

articles.title: Former Obama aides claim Democratic donors are still holding back after being burned by 2024 loss
articles.summary: "Pod Save America" hosts say Democratic donors are holding back despite what they call a generational midterm election opportunity for the party.
articles.body: Former Obama advisers who host the "Pod Save America" podcast spoke Friday about the purported reasons some major Democratic donors are holding back money as the party sees encouraging signs ahead in November's midterm elections. At the Texas Tribune Festival last week, the podcast hosts shared their optimism over Texas turning blue because of Republican struggles in purple states. Dan Pfeiffer spoke about numerous factors working against Republicans, even in rural areas, but still warned that Democrats have far less money to work with, compared to the GOP. Tommy Vietor replied, "I think those spending restraints compared to the opportunity are why you're starting to hear some, you know, sort of operatives and candidates like voicing concern and frustration that some of the traditional like big, big donors of the Democratic Party, are not viewing this as the generational opportunity that it could be." THE SOROS POLITICAL MACHINE IS PUTTING MILLIONS TO WORK BEFORE ELECTION DAY — AND ZEROING IN ON KEY RACES "Because I was talking to someone today who was like, ‘Let me paint for you the like extreme optimistic picture,’ which is Democrats are not only winning on the generic ballot, but if you look at the top like most salient issues, we are crushing in those areas as well, which was not the case in 2024, right?," he continued. Vietor proposed that if the results of this midterm election resemble recent special elections where Democrats overperformed, "it is like truly a historic opportunity to win statewide races, congressional races, down-ballot, up and down. And it just feels like a moment when all the biggest donors in the party should be pushing all their chips in the table as aggressively as possible and not holding back for — I don't know what reason — Trump bothering them?" "Yeah, I think there has been a huge shift in the funding approach ... in the large donor community since 2024," Pfeiffer said. "Part of it is people still angry about how that election went and feeling like they lit a billion dollars on fire in that election, which is a fair quibble in some ways." "There are a lot of people who are very afraid of being targeted by Trump like that just that your business is going to be targeted," he continued. "You're going to have all of a sudden, you're going to the FBI is going to show up at your door. You're going to have regulatory scrutiny you wouldn't have before. And so that has limited money." CASH-STRAPPED DNC SHELLED OUT MORE THAN $800K TO NON-VOTING TERRITORIES LIKE VIRGIN ISLANDS WHILE IN DEBT Pfeiffer argued further that this midterm election could possibly lead to a scenario where "you're looking at one of the largest swings in American history, something where Democrats could pick up races we've never even thought possible," he said. "We've been using 2006 as like the most relevant example of an election because it's you know, it's an unpopular president, unpopular war, all of that. But it very well could be a little more like '94, where everything changes where it's a realigning election." Democratic consultant Julian Epstein rejected the podcasters' comments. "It's always funny to me how these group think 'insiders' parrot one another, even when they're 'consensus' is obviously wrong. The truth is that the so-called 'blue tsunami' is very likely overstated. The margin of error and the 40 battleground congressional districts is more like 2% right now, and we've consistently seen Republicans being undersampled in recent years," he told Fox News Digital. "Donors are holding back because the Democrats don't have any attractive, positive agenda," he continued. "Democrats have an even lower approval rating than the president. Democrats used to be about building; today they are about tax-and-spend redistributionist big government welfare. They are about the victim Olympics." "Try going out on the street and ask 10 voters to name three things Democrats stand [for] today. I doubt you'll find any that can," Epstein added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Republican consultant Mary Marslender suggested the podcasters may have a key point. "Yes, major Democratic donors are holding back, still frustrated by the fallout from the 2024 cycle and increasingly concerned about the party's direction," Marslender told Fox News Digital. "Kamala Harris’ failed presidential campaign spent a staggering $1.5 billion in just 15 weeks, losing the popular vote, the Electoral College, the Senate, the White female vote, and support among both Latino and working-class voters," she continued. "That’s the equivalent of spending $25,000 per hour only to lose nearly every key demographic and benchmark the campaign touted as strengths." "Major donors who contributed eight-figure sums in 2024 have noticed this poor return on investment and appear less willing to spend this cycle," she said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Additionally, many major Democratic donors have slowed or withheld contributions because of concerns about the Party’s shift toward socialist policies," Marslender added. "Unsurprisingly, calls to destroy the country’s financial institutions have not resonated well with wealthy Democratic supporters."

articles.title: Andy Burnham to unveil public body to invest in electricity grid
articles.summary: The prime minister will say he wants to reduce energy costs in his first conference speech as Labour leader.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham is expected to announce a new government body to invest in Britain's electricity grid in his first party conference speech as Labour leader on Tuesday.

The prime minister will tell party activists in Liverpool that the new publicly owned company, branded Great British Grid, will speed up grid hook-ups by driving up competition for connection projects.

Burnham is expected to put the proposals at the heart of a new goal to bring UK energy costs in line with other nations in Europe within ten years.

He will promise to have an "honest conversation" with the public and take on the "difficult issues" that have been ignored for too long.

Burnham is expected to bill the creation of the GB Grid as the first significant move in his ambition to provide greater public control of utilities, which he put at the centre of his pitch for power over the summer.

He is expected to say that faster connections to the electricity grid could help fix a "cost crisis" in energy that has proved "crippling for businesses".

Full details of the new body are yet to be set out, but Labour said it would invest in and compete for transmission connection projects alongside the three private companies that currently own and manage the grid in Britain.

The party said it would also make it easier for firms waiting to be connected to the grid to finance connection infrastructure themselves, with GB Grid supporting and potentially co-investing in projects alongside them.

Labour has said that funding for the new body will be found within the existing budget of GB Energy, the public green investment company set up by Labour last year and which is now headquartered in Aberdeen.

Faster grid hook-ups planned for some green energy projects

Why the PM could finally drop the triple lock pension pledge

The transition of electricity generation from large fossil fuel stations to the more remote locations used for renewables, such as offshore windfarms, will require Britain's ageing transmission grid to undergo extensive rewiring in coming years.

Energy regulator Ofgem has estimated that £70bn of investment is required in the grid between 2025 and 2031, quadrupling the current rate of investment.

But in a report earlier this month, the National Audit Office warned that the number of projects waiting to connect to the grid had grown "significantly" whilst delays to projects were also increasing.

In his speech on Tuesday afternoon, Burnham is expected to say that GB Grid will "work with the private sector and network companies" to "reform a broken energy market".

He will add: "It will increase competition to drive down costs and speed up delivery so businesses can connect faster and grow quicker.

"This is what more public control can do."

Burnham will promise "bold and honest" leadership, saying he will outline policies and commitments that form a "serious prospectus" for Britain and offer people more control over their lives.

He is expected to say that he initially wanted to "give the usual tub-thumping conference speech" but that "the patriot in me tells me something very different is needed".

The prime minister has made "hope" the overall message of the four-day gathering.

It comes ahead of a tricky Budget at the end of next month, where the room for manoeuvre facing the prime minister has been narrowed by recent rises to the cost of UK borrowing.

Ahead of the speech, the prime minister has promised to reveal details of how he intends to fund his plans to provide free social care services to everyone in England.

He has said he wants to put his his plans before voters at the next general election, which legally must be held by August 2029 at the latest, before aiming to roll out the new system from 2030.

There has been speculation that in his efforts to free up future funding for his social care plans, the prime minister could question the long-term sustainability of the "triple lock" uprating policy for the state pension.

The policy - under which pension payments rise annually by the highest of 2.5%, inflation, or average wage rises - is expected to add billions to the cost of pensions in future years because of the UK's ageing population.

Downing Street would not be drawn on whether a review is being considered, while ministers have been clear that a manifesto commitment to keep the triple lock for the duration of this parliament stands.

On Monday, Chancellor John Healey declined to guarantee the promise - which has featured in every Labour manifesto since 2015 - would feature in the party's blueprint for voters at the next election.

"The manifesto will be the manifesto at the time, I'm not going to do that now," he told BBC Radio 5 Live.

Sharon Graham, general secretary of the Unite union, issued a pre-emptive warning that scrapping the triple lock would be "electoral suicide".

articles.title: Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma: The Ugandan journalist who became king amid a succession row
articles.summary: Kijanangoma is being crowned amid a dispute over a young heir whom the royal clan does not recognise.
articles.body:
Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma Nyabongo II, who is set to be crowned king of Uganda's Tooro kingdom later, has long been a familiar face in the country.

For many Ugandans, he was known not as the heir to the throne, but as a storyteller, as a long-serving anchor and editor at the state broadcaster.

But Kijanangoma, 56, has now become the subject of media attention himself - his rise to the Tooro throne sparking controversy and widespread reactions beyond the country.

Tooro is one of Uganda's four main officially recognised historical kingdoms. For the last 31 years, it has been headed by King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who was once known as a "boy king", after ascending to the throne as an infant.

Oyo became king in 1995 at the age of just three, following the death of his father. Then the world's youngest monarch, he ruled until he died last month from cancer, aged just 34.

The coronation is a day for celebration, involving traditional practices starting from midnight. The new king then walks about 4km (2.5 miles) to the official Karuziika royal palace where he is crowned.

A mock fight follows, to signify that kingship does not come easy, and he is then blessed by members of the royal Babiito clan, the Tooro kingdom's Information Minister Charles Mwanguhya told the BBC Focus on Africa podcast.

He performs other ceremonies that signifies his assumption of the throne, before he sits on the throne and an actual crown placed on his head to signify his new authority, his new position as the new Tooro king.

But the selection of Kijanangoma as king was far from straightforward.

According to tradition, a recognised son of the late king should succeed him. Close members of the royal family said Oyo had left a young son and a will with instructions that the child should be next on the throne.

But the son has never been revealed to the public and nor was he recognised by the committee of 21 Babiito clan members who choose the king and eventually selected Kijanangoma.

The late King Oyo was never publicly married, and little is known about his wife or their son.

Nonetheless his mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, argued that the late king's will ought to have been respected.

However, the royal succession committee ignored her wishes, insisting their selection process was conducted in accordance with Tooro customs and traditions.

The new king has thus found himself at the centre of a succession dispute, with Kemigisa and her close relatives unhappy with the outcome.

Kemigisa referred to Kijanangoma's selection as the "announcement of a second king" being "made after the will of King Oyo was read to members of the royal family".

"As a mother, that was extraordinarily painful," she said, describing celebrations for the next king taking place "only metres from where my son's body lay".

The queen later said Oyo's son, who was in the US state of Texas, had been due to return home but that could not happen amid a "tense and polarised succession dispute".

"No child should be placed in circumstances where returning to his father's homeland could mean being drawn into hostility and conflict," Kemigisa asserted in a post on X.

But according to the Tooro kingdom's information minister, the son being talked about "hasn't been presented anywhere, which means there is a growing acceptance that sad as it may be, King Oyo didn't leave a son behind".

While King Oyo inherited the crown from his father, Mwanguhya told the BBC "the crown has moved to a different line within the ruling clan".

A king must come from the Babiito clan, specifically the lineage of King George David Matthew Kamurasi Rukidi III, according to royal palace sources.

Kijanangoma and the late King Oyo are cousins. Both are grandsons of Rukidi III, the 11th king, or Omukama, who ruled the Tooro kingdom from 1928 to 1965.

Kijanangoma was among several people who were considered for the role, including Prince George Desmond Kamurasi, who plays football for one of the UK's best-known amateur clubs .

According to the succession committee, the South East Dons captain and goalkeeper declined the offer of the throne, citing other responsibilities.

After he was formally announced, Kijanangoma promised that the palace would be open to the people, while vowing to focus on unity and development.

"I ask you for one thing - they have given me this title as king but I cannot work alone, I have to work with you," he said.

Uganda's traditional kings have no formal political authority, but they retain cultural influence and command significant loyalty in the communities they lead.

The country is home to four main kingdoms, the largest and most prominent being Buganda in the central region, which encompasses the capital Kampala.

The kingdoms were abolished in 1967, but the government under President Yoweri Museveni restored them in the early 1990s.

The government said this was to promote cultural pride and national unity, but the move has also been interpreted as a way of appeasing communities and fostering political loyalty.

Amid the succession dispute, the government backed the Babiito clan's choice of Kijanangoma. Attorney General Sam Mayanja said the Tooro kingdom was cleared to go ahead with the coronation, as there had not been a formal complaint against him.

The date of the coronation was announced by the government and Museveni is scheduled to attend.

The president's son and the head of the military, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, has also publicly supported Kijanangoma. "Long may he reign," he posted on X.

Kijanangoma's very name points to his royal heritage.

His father, the first Kijanangoma, was born in the year King Rukidi III became king. The king gave him the name, which means the "one who comes with the royal drum".

The drum of royalty, foretold two generations earlier, is now returning to its bearer.

Kijanangoma was born in 1970 and raised at their family home at Kidukuru village in Fort Portal, about 300 km (186 miles) from Kampala.

He left the village to pursue further studies and graduated with a mass communication degree from Uganda's prestigious Makerere University in 1999.

He worked as a broadcaster in a career spanning more than two decades, including in neighbouring Rwanda and at home, with the Uganda Broadcasting Corporation.

The years spent engaging with the public, the interactions with leaders and the exposure to national affairs in his work as a journalist may yet serve him well as he returns to the community he came from, this time as their leader.

After he was named king, Kijanangoma said he would use the connections he had built up over 21 years working as a journalist "to get good things for our people".

His mother, Assimwe Yusta Kijanangoma, is confident that he is well prepared for his new role. She says his upbringing was deeply rooted in tradition.

"I really raised him with the teachings of the old kingdom of a cane and instructions and scolding. I laugh with him, and other times I scold him," she told the BBC.

She added: "Eddy is well-mannered, he does not fight, or shout, even when wronged, he says a few words and does not go so much into it."

She feels good for her son, although she admits to having mixed emotions, especially as her son is taking over after the death of a "great man".

articles.title: Won't reopen Sohrabuddin case but will test validity of acquittal of all accused: SC
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: SC Monday agreed to test the validity of acquittal of police officers and all other accused concurrently by the trial court and Bombay high
articles.body: NEW DELHI: SC Monday agreed to test the validity of acquittal of police officers and all other accused concurrently by the trial court and Bombay high court in the controversial 2005 Sohrabuddin fake encounter case.Appearing for petitioner Rubabuddin Sheikh, brother of Sohrabuddin, senior advocate D Seshadri Naidu told a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana that his client lost his brother, sister-in-law and brother's friend Tulsiram Prajapati yet the trial court and the HC overlooked critical evidence to acquit all 22 accused, 21 of them police officers from Gujarat, Rajasthan and Andhra Pradesh.The CJI-led bench said it would not reopen the case relating to fake encounter killings of Sohrabuddin, who had multiple criminal cases pending against him, or Prajapati, but would examine the strength of testimonies of witnesses.Appearing for some of the acquitted accused, senior advocate K Parameshwar told the bench that HC, in its appellate capacity, had considered the testimony of each of the witnesses before approving the acquittals.The bench asked the CBI and the petitioner to flag important witnesses and their depositions to the SC on the next date of hearing while seeking responses from the acquitted accused to the appeal filed by Rubabuddin.Justice Bagchi said, "It is worrisome that there has been wholesale turning hostile of witnesses. More worrisome is the fact that those who had recorded their statements before the magistrate under Section 164 of Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC), they also turned hostile."The petitioner said the high court had failed to discharge its appellate function especially when it was informed in no uncertain terms that the evidence was tainted because of a "tailored investigation" which was aggravated by the actions of an "unprincipled prosecutor".Sohrabuddin and his wife Kauser Bi, along with Prajapati, were allegedly abducted by a team of Gujarat and Rajasthan police in Oct 2005. While Prajapati was allowed to go, Sohrabuddin was killed in a fake encounter, and his wife was allegedly murdered. Prajapati was killed in another fake encounter a year later.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: These are only byelections, says CJI as SC declines urgent hearing on WB SIR pleas
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Monday declined to advance the hearing of pleas concerning the pendency of appeals arising from the Special Intensive Revision
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Monday declined to advance the hearing of pleas concerning the pendency of appeals arising from the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in West Bengal.Byelections in Rejinagar and Nandigram assembly constituencies in the state will be held on Oct 6. A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said the matter would be taken up on Oct 5. The matter was mentioned for urgent hearing after it was stated that the case, earlier expected to be heard on Sept 29, was now tentatively listed for Oct 5.Seeking an earlier hearing, the lawyer said more than 18,000 appeals against the exclusion of names from the electoral rolls were still pending before appellate tribunals constituted pursuant to the SC's directions."There are more than 18,000 appeals pending... These people did not take part in the first elections," the counsel said, adding that the affected voters could miss out on exercising their franchise for a second time.The counsel said that the Oct 6 bypolls were scheduled immediately after the proposed Oct 5 hearing and urged the court to take up the matter earlier."These are only by-elections," CJI Surya Kant said, adding that the matter would be taken up on Oct 5.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: On deadlines, we must also look within: Supreme Court
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: On a petition seeking direction to West Bengal speaker to expeditiously decide the disqualification petitions against rebel TMC MLAs, SC Monday
articles.body: NEW DELHI: On a petition seeking direction to West Bengal speaker to expeditiously decide the disqualification petitions against rebel TMC MLAs, SC Monday said before setting a deadline for other constitutional authorities, the judiciary must introspect whether it conformed to statutory deadlines for adjudication of cases.When senior advocate Kapil Sibal pressed for seeking a response from the office of the speaker on the three-month-old disqualification petitions, a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said it will dispose of the petition asking the Supreme Court to abide by its 2020 judgement in Keisham Meghachandra Singh case, fixing a three-month deadline for a decision by the speaker.Sibal said he had no problem with this order but requested the court to examine the set pattern in which speakers delay a decision on disqualification petitions placing a premium to defections.Justice Bagchi said, "We should hold the mirror to ourselves before giving directions. There are so many statutes that require the judiciary to conclude proceedings within a timeframe. We are gloriously in breach of these."The disqualifications were filed on July 8 by TMC against 10 rebel MLAs who formed a separate block.The three-month time period for the speaker to decide the disqualification petitions ends on Oct 8.The CJI-headed bench said, "We have every reason to believe that the speaker of the legislative assembly is fully cognisant of the principles stated in the Keisham Meghachandra Singh ruling and will make all endeavour to take an appropriate decision within that framework."Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Be like Sophie Cunningham, not Chris Simms — never give in to the outrage mob
articles.summary: Sophie Cunningham's refusal to back down after WNBA backlash stands in stark contrast to Chris Simms and other sports figures who caved to outrage.
articles.body: Sophie Cunningham understands something that very few others in the sports world seem to. You never, ever cave to the mob if you haven't done anything wrong. The Indiana Fever guard proved as much this summer after she came out against biological males competing against females in sports. SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SPARKS SOCIAL MEDIA MELTDOWN BY SPEAKING OUT TO PROTECT WOMEN'S SPORTS Her stance prompted her to garner the title "MAGA Barbie." It sparked fans to boo her when she entered the game in cities such as Seattle. It caused a sports reporter to say that she is "unafraid to be blatantly transphobic" and fans to call for her suspension. Did Cunningham buckle? Hell no. She doubled down with an Instagram post that declared she isn't backing down for anyone. "I said what I said," she wrote. This is the only way to do it. If there's one thing the mob hates more than anything, it's courage. You show it to them, they go away. It's just sad that so few seem to possess it. NBC Sports football analyst Chris Simms was the latest to bow to online outrage over some perfectly reasonable comments. After Oregon quarterback Dante Moore was knocked out of Saturday's game due to a helmet-to-helmet hit by USC's Desman Stephens II, Simms did what an analyst is paid to do: analyze. At halftime, Simms said that Moore's injury was a "Debbie Downer" moment because fans want to see teams at full strength. He then shared some advice his father told him about how to "make sure you get down in time and don't take any big hits." He added how Moore's late slide put Stephens in a "no-win situation." DAN DAKICH CALLS CHRIS SIMMS' APOLOGY OVER DANTE MOORE SLIDE ANALYSIS 'SOFT A-- BULLS--T' This is an ex-football player talking football. But apparently all Oregon fans wanted to hear was that this was the dirtiest hit in the history of the sport, so Sunday, Simms took to social media to write "I clearly did not show enough sympathy for the situation. I mishandled the situation and I was wrong. I'm sorry for that." It seems like we see a new one of these every week. Earlier this month, Texas quarterback Arch Manning laughed at an AI meme of ESPN reporter Holly Rowe getting slapped by Longhorns coach Steve Sarkisian. He was shamed into apologizing two days later. In July, Sandy Brondello, coach of the WNBA's Toronto Tempo, wanted a foul to be called on Atlanta's Angel Reese, and could be heard telling refs that Reese was a "protected species." This is common lingo in Australia — Brondello's home country — where it's meant to express frustration over a player getting special treatment. But Brondello still issued a written apology to Reese, saying "I used a phrase that I shouldn't have used, and I take full responsibility for that." And then, of course, there was Lions receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown caving last year after doing the Trump dance after a touchdown in a game vs. Commanders. Said St. Brown: "First of all, if I offended anyone, I do apologize. I did not mean to offend anyone. It was just, we're having fun." It's hard watching these sports figures shed their dignity with each one of these mea culpas. What they don't understand is that they are losing respect from the public every time they issue one. The outrage mob simply sees them as people who will fold the next time they want to sink their hooks into them. And the folks who would have supported them if they stood strong? They now see a spineless pushover. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! This doesn't mean that people should never apologize. During his time in Seattle, Richard Sherman was infamous for his inability to ever take accountability for his wrongdoing. That's also a form of weakness — it's just wearing a different costume. But to surrender when you've done nothing wrong? It's not noble, it's nauseating. CHARLES BARKLEY DECLARES WNBA IS 'FOR WOMEN ONLY' AFTER ONGOING TRANSGENDER ATHLETE DEBATE People like Cunningham know this. Charles Barkley, too. The Hall of Fame hooper is on record saying trans athletes don't belong in women's sports, and the blowback has been almost nonexistent because everyone knows he is going to hold firm in his position. That's the power of integrity. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The vocal minority shouldn't have the influence that it does. Yet it regularly turns titans of the sports world into mush. Don't be like Chris Simms, who gave into the mob. Be like Cunningham, who decided to stand up to it. Sophie's choice is the only choice.

articles.title: Michigan Dem Abdul El-Sayed wants Bill Maher to get his 'a-- whooped' if invited on show
articles.summary: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed told Chuck Todd he'd want Bill Maher's "a-- whooped" on "Real Time" if he were invited onto the HBO show.
articles.body: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed told former NBC News host Chuck Todd on Friday that he would want to go on comedian Bill Maher's show to see his "a-- whooped" after his anti-Islam comments. During the "Noosphere" interview, El-Sayed said he'd be willing to appear on Maher or Joe Rogan's respective shows despite them espousing what he considered to be "terrible" beliefs because he'd want to speak with their audiences. In addition, El-Sayed claimed that he'd be willing to go on "Real Time" in order to watch Maher get his "a-- whooped" by a Muslim. HASAN PIKER ACCUSES BILL MAHER OF BEING AN 'ISLAMOPHOBE' AND DEMONSTRATING 'ANTI-BLACKNESS' "You know how many terrible things Bill Maher has said about people like me?" El-Sayed said. "Terrible, awful things. Of course, he's still got his show on Comedy Central, and everybody seems to be perfectly okay going on that show despite the fact that he said deeply terrible things." "But you know who else would go on that show?" he continued. "I would go on that show. You know why? A: I wanna give people the image of watching him get his a-- whooped on his own show by a guy who prays like I do. And I'd also go on the show because I want to convince the people who watch his show, right, that a lot of the things that he says, just not viable." Maher responded to El-Sayed's comments during his show on Friday and offered an invitation for the Michigan Democrat to appear on "Real Time." "It’s not people like you, I would love to have you on, sir, by the way," Maher said. "And I hope we can make that happen. I talk about Islam. It’s never personal, and it’s never about race. It’s about ideas. Religion is an opinion. That’s all religion is: a group of thoughts that form an opinion of something. I have different views on what, you know, how women should be treated and things like that, that we will discuss. I hope you will accept our invitation." ABDUL EL-SAYED GRILLED ON PAST STATEMENTS ON SHARIA LAW AND WHITE SUPREMACY, TAXING THE RICH Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed's campaign and Maher's representative for comment but did not immediately receive a response. El-Sayed has frequently invoked aggressive language against his GOP rival Mike Rogers. Last month, El-Sayed challenged Rogers to a game of tackle football despite being more than 20 years younger than the Republican candidate. "Since you’re too afraid to debate me, how about you ‘hold me accountable’ on a football field instead," El-Sayed wrote on X. "Tackle, no pads like we used to play when we were kids. I’d be happy to show you [how] much I love football." Speaking to Fox News correspondent Alexis McAdams earlier this month, Rogers dismissed the comment as "unserious" in light of real election issues. You think about what the problems are here. People are facing this affordability [sic] credit. He wants to thump his chest and show how macho he is, and he spends a lot of time talking about high school. This is not about high school," Rogers said.

articles.title: Africa’s space ambitions are moving from policy to practice
articles.summary: As the Africa Space Expo closes in Abidjan, African innovators are showing what the continent can build.
articles.body:
Accra, Ghana – The Africa Space Expo (ASPEX), which closed in Abidjan, Ivory Coast, last week, was not designed as a showcase for rockets and astronauts. Organisers presented it instead as a marketplace for space applications in food security, climate resilience, territorial monitoring, connectivity and maritime security, bringing start-ups, project labs and investors together to move ideas from demonstration to deployment.

The event also produced several concrete agreements. The Ivory Coast signed the Artemis Accords, becoming the 75th signatory of the agreement on space exploration and development, while Angola signed a letter of intent on space cooperation with the United Arab Emirates.

But beyond the agreements, the expo highlighted a question that is becoming harder to avoid: Can Africa move from using space technology to building more of it itself?

Ghana offers a clear illustration of both the progress and the gap.

Ghana’s ambitions in space and nuclear science date back to its early years of independence. In 1961, President Kwame Nkrumah’s government initiated a nuclear reactor project in Accra. Two years later, the government established the Ghana Atomic Energy Commission through an act of Parliament with a mandate covering the peaceful applications of nuclear energy.

The reactor project was shelved after Nkrumah was overthrown in 1966, but the institution he helped establish remains the parent body of the Ghana Space Science and Technology Institute (GSSTI).

Joseph Tandoh, director of the GSSTI, traces Ghana’s more recent space programme to a partnership with South Africa.

“Ghana became a partner through South Africa,” he told Al Jazeera. “Through that project, we were able to reconstruct the old satellite antenna at Kuntunse into a radio telescope.”

Through its partnership with South Africa on radio astronomy, Ghana converted a redundant 32-metre (105ft) antenna at Kuntunse into a functioning radio telescope. Ghana became the first of South Africa’s eight African Square Kilometre Array partner countries to complete the conversion, and the telescope was launched in August 2017.

Ghana’s National Space Policy was approved by the cabinet in 2022 and launched in 2024. The government approved the establishment of a Ghana Space Agency in 2025, beginning the process of creating a dedicated national institution for the sector.

The institutional framework is taking shape. The harder question is how Ghana moves from using space technology to developing and building more of it itself.

At the GSSTI, that transition is already under way.

Tandoh told Al Jazeera GEOMAIZE, a partnership between the GSSTI and VITO, the Flemish Institute for Technological Research in Belgium, has demonstrated how satellite data can be applied to Ghanaian agriculture.

The project monitored crop health and developed algorithms to classify crops. Ghana is also expanding its use of Earth observation data and artificial intelligence for crop monitoring and yield prediction.

But predicting yields has proved more difficult. Tandoh said the model’s accuracy fell short of expectations, largely because many Ghanaian farmers practise smallholder mixed cropping and satellite soil-moisture data are too coarse to capture differences between small farms.

A follow-up project supported by the French embassy and international research partners, is now working to improve the estimates.

The GSSTI has also used satellite data to track forest loss linked to mining and is working with partners in Nigeria on a digital twin to simulate coastal erosion at Keta and Agavedzi. Japanese cooperation has provided technical training while the French government supported work on space legislation that produced a draft now being reviewed by the attorney general.

“We always say that Ghana Space Science and Technology Institute becoming an agency is to position Ghana in a way that we will not only be users of the technology but we will also contribute to designing, developing and building our own tools,” Tandoh said.

Victor Tagborloh founded Galaxy Aerospace Ghana in 2020. Two years later, his team launched a high-altitude balloon into near space, capturing images of Ghana’s geography with clearance from national security and airport authorities.

The company has since designed mini-rockets for the GSSTI, trained young people in space robotics and artificial intelligence and pushed for the introduction of Starlink in Ghana in 2024.

But Tagborloh said the company has yet to secure an investor, six years after it was founded.

Galaxy’s longer-term plans include a space university on 33,000 hectares (82,000 acres) that it has secured at Apam in Ghana’s Central Region as well as a ground station that would give the country greater capacity to monitor floods, mining activity and coastal erosion.

The company is seeking investors for the ground station and a geospatial intelligence platform. Tagborloh said the curriculum is ready and the land is available. What is missing is the capital to turn those plans into infrastructure.

He also argued that Ghana’s position near the equator could provide an advantage for launching spacecraft, potentially reducing the fuel required to reach orbit. Several other African countries share similar geography.

But Tagborloh’s ambition goes beyond launching rockets. He wants Ghana to develop more of the infrastructure and expertise needed to build its own space capabilities.

Bright Atsu Sogbey, president of the Africa Development Council and a senior research engineer at the Ghana Atomic Energy Commission, argued that the private sector cannot build the industry alone.

“Borrowed technology cannot be sustainable,” Sogbey told Al Jazeera. “The state must be in the driver’s seat, using the natural resources we have to ensure that, in partnership with the private sector, we can have laboratories and manufacturing hubs for the space industry.”

He pointed to South Africa, Egypt and Nigeria, which have established space laboratories and manufactured test satellites. Ghana, he said, still lacks the state-backed laboratories and manufacturing hubs needed to produce more of its own components rather than importing them.

“Enough of the talk shop,” Sogbey said. “The next expo should see African satellites assembled on this continent and launching capability for African satellites.”

Engineer Daniel Aboagye, CEO of African Progressive Research and Innovations, said the change must also begin in education.

“With how technology is advancing, Africa must introduce space science into its education systems,” Aboagye told Al Jazeera. “We cannot continue to be consumers of technology we do not understand.”

Kwadwo Dwomo II, CEO of COMCENT Ghana, works on agritech systems that depend on satellite data. He also called for greater government investment in the sector.

Ghana is home to a small cluster of companies, including Galaxy Aerospace, Xavier Space Solutions and Ayeji Aerospace, working in areas such as satellite technology, Earth observation and geospatial services.

Galaxy Aerospace confirmed to Al Jazeera that it was unable to participate in this year’s expo. The company said it hopes to participate in the next expo.

The challenge facing Ghana is shared across much of Africa: moving from using space technology to developing and building more of it locally while overcoming limited investment, infrastructure and manufacturing capacity.

ASPEX was designed in part to address that gap.

The African Space Agency, headquartered in Egypt, is intended to provide a continental framework for cooperation while the expo aims to connect investors with African start-ups, researchers and space projects.

But the distance between the ambitions presented at the expo and the resources available to engineers trying to turn them into businesses remains substantial.

For Tandoh, Ghana’s immediate priority is to build the application layer: a satellite-data processing hub capable of serving ministries across government before the country moves further into designing and launching its own satellites.

“Space cuts across all the ministries,” he told Al Jazeera. “We should be able to build and validate our own tools first.”

For Tagborloh, the timeline is more urgent.

“We shouldn’t wait for tomorrow,” he told Al Jazeera. “Whatever decision we have to take, especially for human resource capital in the space industry, it has to be now.”

Ghana has the policy. It has engineers, research institutions and companies trying to build a space industry. What it does not yet have is the capital and manufacturing capacity to turn those capabilities into a domestic industry.

“We have the team, the knowledge, the research and the technical know-how,” Tagborloh told Al Jazeera. “We just need funds.”

articles.title: More attempts at longer migrant small boat crossings in Channel
articles.summary: The government says it is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings.
articles.body:
A growing number of migrants are trying to cross the Channel on small boats using longer routes from beaches further south and west of Calais and Dunkirk, French authorities say.

Last week one boat set off from Normandy and spent more than 30 hours at sea , before being intercepted and taken to Dover by Border Force.

Although attempts from Normandy have been rare, authorities in neighbouring Seine-Maritime say there have already been 58 attempts this year, up from 30 last year.

The government says it is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings, with figures showing a sharp drop in arrivals this year .

Despite overall crossings dropping , the stretch of coastline used for smuggling appears to be widening.

Earlier this month another migrant boat was met by lifeboats from the Isle of Wight having set off from the Cherbourg area.

These locations are nearly 80 miles (128 km) from the beaches where many of the small boats have crossed in recent years, with those on board spending longer at sea.

Audrey Baconnais-Rosez, the local government representative in Seine-Maritime, said: "The number of attempts to cross the Channel has increased in number and it is getting further and further from the north of France."

She added that authorities were "managing to stop half of them".

The number of gendarmes patrolling the coast within Dieppe and further to nearly the Le Havre area have been increased, she said.

"Nowadays it's about 50 gendarmes on the coast and we have nearly 20 police officers in Dieppe and the surrounding [area] to try to stop them," she said.

Baconnais-Rosez also said some smugglers were still attempting to use ferries to Newhaven in Sussex.

"We are still intercepting them and we are bringing them to justice as well," she added.

Dr Peter Walsh, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford's Migration Observatory, says it is highly plausible that the new routes are due to police disrupting boat launches in northern France.

"It's not at all optimal for these boats to set off so far away from their intended destination," he said.

"Some of these journeys would not be 20 miles (32km) but 50 miles (80km) or even more, which substantially increases the danger of course on board the boats."

David McFarlane, a marine safety consultant, said the longer the voyage, the more risk of encountering hazardous sea conditions.

"If a low pressure system is developing over the Atlantic, it can mean that in advance of the winds picking up, a swell will start to increase, with the increased likelihood of sea sickness for some, which can lead to dehydration," he said.

"The wind of course can pick up very quickly and waves can get up to 3.5m (11ft) in height in the Channel.

"This increases the risk of the boat being swamped by sea water, with the obvious danger to human life by drowning or exposure."

So far, 2026 has seen 19,135 people make the Channel crossing, compared to 32,188 during the same period in 2025.

However, the Home Secretary ordered a review last week after two migrant vessels reached the Kent coast unintercepted .

A total of 781 migrants arrived in 10 small boats on Wednesday , the highest number for a single day this year, according to Home Office figures.

Tony Smith, the former director general of Border Force, said the smugglers would continue to adapt.

"We've seen the Normandy crossings and the undetected crossings," he said.

"They're not going to give up as long as the business model continues to exist and there's a market to bring migrants over from France.

"Every successful landing is a message to the next migrant waiting on a French beach that it's worth a try."

A Home Office spokesperson said joint efforts had seen more than 48,000 crossing attempts prevented and 1,100 boats and engines seized since the election.

"Our efforts are having an impact, with the number of small boat crossings down significantly this year and the lowest number recorded for the month of July since 2020," they added.

"But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches, along with a surge unit of 45 additional officers to bolster action in Western coastal areas."

articles.title: Cornell rape accuser’s attorney says the school and law enforcement failed a young woman
articles.summary: The DA vows to pursue any additional evidence after the woman’s lawsuit prompted him to reopen the case.
articles.body: The attorney representing a former Cornell University student who said she was gang-raped for hours in 2024 after she was pressured to take ketamine decried the initial investigation and accused both law enforcement officials and the school of failing his client. “She was a young woman who went to Cornell with high hopes, thought that this was her dream come true, and then that didn’t happen,” Thomas P. Giuffra told NBC News on Monday. “Now she’s not in college. She’s not pursuing her goals, and she’s just trying to hang on.” In a written statement Monday, the woman, identified only as Jane Doe, said she hopes “to recover from this trauma but it is extremely difficult. It affects every aspect of my life. It will haunt me and be part of me the rest of my life.” In a civil lawsuit filed this month, Doe alleges that Chi Phi fraternity brothers sexually assaulted her and that one sent a message encouraging other members to participate in the attack. The fraternity chapter was subsequently barred from campus, but no one was criminally charged. According to the lawsuit, some of the students were able to “mitigate their conduct” by writing essays to the university. “Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false,” Kyle Kimball, Cornell’s vice president for university relations, said in a statement. Giuffra told NBC News that in the days following the alleged assault, his client was “traumatized, numb and unable to function or accept the horror of what had happened.” She was in “self-preservation mode,” he said, and had faith that university officials would investigate her claims thoroughly. “She wanted to give Cornell the opportunity to make this right, because this was her expectation. So she didn’t want to start a lawsuit,” he said. She filed the civil lawsuit, which names the Chi Phi chapter, Chi Phi National and Cornell University among others, this month. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said that prompted him to reopen the case and consider whether to bring charges related to the 2024 allegations. The university said Monday that it supports Van Houten’s decision to have the case heard before a criminal grand jury. “Now that this lawsuit has been filed, that raises the question that Jane Doe believes there’s additional evidence,” Van Houten told NBC News on Monday. “We want to talk to her. We want to flesh out with her what that additional evidence is.” He promised to pursue any new evidence “zealously.” “We understand that with human beings, especially processing trauma, it takes time sometimes to fully grasp and understand and process something that happened to you, and so we recognize that even though it’s been two years and we haven’t heard from her since then or her attorneys, that it’s never too late to reopen and pursue justice when there is additional evidence,” Van Houten said. He said he looks forward to working with the woman before the case is sent to a grand jury. “We want to prepare with her, so she’s comfortable and feels confident that we are going to cover all the bases with her and support her,” Van Houten said. According to Giuffra, his client went to the Cornell University Police Department after the alleged attack but did not speak with anyone beyond the first person who took her report. University officers failed to follow up on key pieces of evidence, including the group chat, Giuffra said. “That available evidence was there. They could have utilized it,” he told NBC News. “What they should have done is investigated who was on that group chat and interviewed witnesses and developed evidence. That’s what investigators do, and that was not done at all.” Ithaca police did not immediately respond to a request for information about their involvement in the case. The Ithaca Police Department is actively investigating the allegations, according to the civil lawsuit. Cornell police referred NBC News to the university’s previous statements defending how it handled the allegations. Cornell pushed back on the suggestion that those involved in the incident faced few consequences at the time, saying in a statement Monday that the university’s Title IX proceedings resulted in a range of sanctions, including expulsions and suspensions. The lawsuit names seven Chi Phi fraternity members. Scott Kretzschmar is among them. An attorney for Kretzschmar strongly denied the accusations and said his client welcomed the new investigation. “The lawsuit against Scott Kretzachmar is not only intentionally dishonest but morally repugnant,” attorney Jeremy Saland said in a statement. “While Scott responded to and made an immature comment on Snapchat, he did nothing else. Nothing.” NBC News tried to contact the six others named in the lawsuit but was not immediately able to reach them or did not receive responses.

articles.title: Maharashtra anti-conversion: New law is changing how Indian Christians pray in the state
articles.summary: A new anti-conversion law in Maharashtra is raising questions about faith, choice and freedom.
articles.body:
Some churches in and around India's financial capital Mumbai have begun asking worshippers to give a declaration in writing - "I came here to pray of my own free will."

Visitors write down their names, sometimes add an ID card number, and sign to say that nobody forced or enticed them to attend church. The forms, a copy of which the BBC has seen, have no official standing. Churches keep them in case a prayer meeting is challenged and its organisers are accused of trying to convert those inside.

The practice began at some churches in late August, just before a new law against religious conversion took effect in Maharashtra state, of which Mumbai is the capital.

The law prohibits religious conversions brought about by force, fraud, coercion or inducement. It also requires people who want to convert voluntarily to notify authorities in advance. An unlawful conversion can lead to a prison sentence of up to seven years, rising to 10 for a repeat offence.

Maharashtra's government says the law protects people, particularly those who are socially or economically vulnerable, from being forced or deceived into changing their religion.

But critics say its broad definitions, severe penalties and scrutiny of even voluntary conversions risk drawing the state and the police into one of the most private decisions a person can make. The state government did not respond to the BBC's repeated requests for comment.

While the law applies to all religions, the anxiety is being felt most deeply at places where minorities, especially Christians, worship. At the heart of the debate is a long-running tension over allegations, usually made by right-wing groups, about people being coerced or induced to change their religion for benefits.

Devdan Tribhuvan has seen some of that anxiety up close.

A fourth-generation Christian in Vasai, a suburb of Mumbai, he is part of an organisation that provides legal aid to Christians in and around the city. In recent months, he says, people have increasingly approached him not about court cases, but with accounts of disrupted prayer meetings and questions about what they are still free to do.

Some have described strangers walking into churches and questioning those inside: "What is your name? Why are you here? Has anyone offered you something?"

The questions can become more pointed, Tribhuvan said, when a worshipper has a name that does not sound Christian: "Has anyone forced you to come? Has anyone offered you an inducement?"

Many who contact him are not looking to take legal action. They want to know whether simply gathering to pray could leave them vulnerable to an accusation of conversion.

In July, an investigation by The Indian Express documented five disruptions of Christian prayer meetings around Mumbai between April and July. Nine police cases followed - seven against worshippers or prayer organisers, and two against members of the Hindu nationalist group Bajrang Dal. Police did not respond to detailed questions about the cases or the action taken.

"Is gathering for prayer itself conversion?" Tribhuvan asks.

In Mumbai, Tribhuvan's question carries particular weight. The city grew by drawing people from across India and beyond, bringing their gods and rituals with them. A church bell can sound within earshot of a mosque's call to prayer; a shrine belonging to one faith can draw followers of another.

People of many faiths make their way to the Muslim shrine Haji Ali. Hindus light candles at Mount Mary, a Catholic basilica overlooking the city. Crowds fill the streets around Lalbaug during the Hindu festival of Ganesh Chaturthi and stream to Siddhivinayak temple throughout the year.

Maharashtra is the latest of more than a dozen states to restrict religious conversion. The laws differ, but their reach has expanded in recent years, particularly in states governed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party. Several are being challenged before the Supreme Court.

Behind that expansion lie claims long made by Hindu nationalist groups, that Christians use money, schooling or medical care to draw poor and tribal communities away from Hinduism, and that Muslim men court Hindu women to convert them - an alleged conspiracy they call "love jihad."

Critics say such accusations have fuelled harassment of Christian prayer meetings and interfaith couples, and that the laws give those making them a way to draw the police into questions of prayer, marriage and belief.

Maharashtra's government says the new law leaves people free to convert by choice, while addressing what it says is a rise in forced conversions that existing laws have failed to curb.

Critics question where it draws the line between force and choice.

"We do not support forceful conversions, if any," said Samsuddin Tamboli, president of the Muslim Satyashodhak Mandal (Muslim Truth-seeking Society), a reformist organisation. His concern is what the law counts as inducement.

Its definition of "allurement" includes employment, free education at a religious institution, a promise of marriage, a "better lifestyle" and "divine healing". Even glorifying one religion over another can fall within it.

"The definition has been kept so vague that almost any benefit accruing to a person can be considered or argued to be an allurement," said Abhay Thipsay, a retired Bombay High Court judge.

"If a person receives some benefit and consciously chooses to convert for that reason, why should it be considered wrong?"

The law also allows parents, siblings and other relatives to complain to police about an allegedly unlawful conversion, leaving the person accused of causing or assisting it to prove that it was lawful.

Critics say for interfaith couples, that provision adds another potential obstacle to marriages that can already face family opposition.

Indian law allows people of different faiths to marry without converting, but requires a month's notice. Lara Jesani, a lawyer who has helped interfaith couples obtain court protection, said details of planned weddings have sometimes reached relatives and Hindu nationalist groups opposed to them within that notice period.

In cases she has handled, she said, families have taken women away, even from the marriage registrar's office.

Now, she fears the new law may give the families or right-wing organisations a new way to target such couples.

"Even when neither intend to convert, [the couples] fear a relative could accuse one partner of trying to convert the other."

The Maharashtra government did not respond to detailed questions from the BBC about these concerns. But when the law was passed, state minister Pankaj Bhoyar said it did not infringe upon the right to change religion. The notification requirement, he said, was intended to establish whether a conversion was voluntary, while allowing the state to act against those brought about by fraud, coercion or inducement.

But Tribhuvan is still worried, an anxiety, he says, which reaches even the small prayer gatherings held closer to home when a church is too far away.

Fifty people might attend, he said, sometimes 100 - and someone who is not Christian might join too.

"If someone else wishes to come and pray, we cannot stop them," he said. "That is what we call the right to choose."

To Thipsay, the retired judge, the precaution points to a larger question.

"If an adult has the power to make major decisions - such as whom to marry - and has been given the right to vote," he said, "why should they not have the power to make this decision too?"

articles.title: Hungary lifts immunity of Prime Minister Magyar, two Orban-era ministers
articles.summary: Hungary’s Parliament lifts immunity of incumbent leader and two former ministers, clearing the way for criminal probes.
articles.body:
Hungary’s Parliament has stripped Prime Minister Peter Magyar and two ministers in former leader Viktor Orban’s nationalist government of their immunity, clearing the way for prosecutors to pursue separate criminal investigations into each of them.

The vote on Monday came after Magyar, who is being investigated for theft, specifically asked for his immunity to be lifted so he could clear himself of “character assassination”. The probes against the Orban-era ministers – who are suspected of embezzlement and bribery – are the first corruption investigations against top government figures from Orban’s 16 years in power.

Legislators voted overwhelmingly in favour of lifting their immunity.

Orban’s Fidesz party and its ally KDNP boycotted the session.

The vote was in response to a request last week from prosecutors seeking to investigate Magyar, as well as former Minister of Culture Balazs Hanko and former Minister of National Development Miklos Sesztak.

Magyar is being investigated over an incident at a Budapest nightclub in June 2024, when prosecutors allege he took a mobile phone from a man filming him and threw it into the Danube River.

Magyar has called the case a “sham” and last week accused prosecutors of trying “to conflate” the ex-ministers’ cases “with the attempt at political character assassination… which has already failed several times”.

Hanko, a legislator from Orban’s Fidesz party, is accused of embezzling more than 40 million euros ($46m) in public funds. Prosecutors allege the money was used to help finance the 2026 parliamentary election campaign and for the personal benefit of others.

Sesztak, a lawmaker from KDNP, is under investigation over allegedly accepting more than $37.2m in bribes and kickbacks connected to vehicle procurements under Hungary’s state bus company, as well as to state construction projects.

The cases come less than six months after Magyar’s Tisza party ended Orban’s 16 years in power with a landslide election victory. Magyar campaigned on pledges to tackle corruption, restore rule-of-law safeguards, and rebuild Hungary’s strained relationship with the European Union.

His government has since made fighting alleged corruption and overpriced public procurement a central part of its programme, including plans for a new asset-recovery office focused on wrongdoing linked to the Orban era.

articles.title: Contradicting Trump, Pope Leo says artificial intelligence safety concerns aren’t ‘fake news’
articles.summary: Pope Leo had identified AI as one of the biggest challenges to humanity within days of his election and took the unusual step of personally launching his own encyclical alongside one of Anthropic’s co-founders at a Vatican event in May.
articles.body: ABOARD THE PAPAL PLANE — Pope Leo XIV said Monday that concerns about artificial intelligence going rogue are not “fake news” and should be taken seriously, insisting that safety issues raised by AI experts should be discussed and acted on. Leo, who dedicated his first encyclical to AI and protecting humanity in its wake, was asked during a press conference about what the United States and China especially should be doing to prevent AI from posing catastrophic risks to humanity. President Donald Trump has called concerns about AI going rogue a “hoax.” “This is a problem that, I think, we need to sit down and talk about,” the American pope told reporters returning home from France. “We can’t just sit back and pretend nothing is going to happen.” Trump has been a champion of AI, often warning that the United States must remain ahead of China in the technological arms race. He has said efforts to limit the technology were part of a “conspiracy” by his political opponents. Several AI giants, including Anthropic, have called for a slowdown in development to give safety measures time to catch up to the fast-moving technology. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, for example, has warned that within six to 12 months, AI could be capable of leading a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet. Trump had a late-night dinner with Amodei on Sunday, during which they discussed Americans’ concerns about the technology and how to keep America dominant, the White House said. “If someone were to ask me am I in panic mode, no, I’m not. I sleep at night,” Leo said. “I do think that the concerns raised by many of the experts, specialists in AI, should be taken seriously.” “I don’t think that that is ‘fake news’ as some have said to try and cause whether financial or other some other kind of benefit,” Leo said. The pope says AI is one of the biggest challenges to humanity The pope, who called for robust regulation of AI and a slowdown of the technology in his encyclical “Magnificent Humanity,” is up to speed on developments in the field. Despite being at the end of a grueling four-day trip to France, Leo noted a news report Monday afternoon about Nvidia introducing guardrails into AI. He also noted that the company has previously resisted outside regulation of AI development. Leo had identified AI as one of the biggest challenges to humanity within days of his election and took the unusual step of personally launching his own encyclical alongside Anthropic’s co-founder Christopher Olah at a Vatican event in May. The initiative was part of the Vatican’s effort to engage Silicon Valley about the human costs of AI. “We need to continue to invite political leaders, leaders of AI, social organizations, associations to come together and look at what is happening already and what could be down the road,” he said Monday. “To simply say, ‘Oh it’s not going to happen,’ and close our eyes to it I think is probably not the most responsible way to go about that,” he added. It’s not the first time the pope and Trump have disagreed With his comments Monday about the legitimacy of safety concerns and AI development, Leo has confirmed another area of disagreement with Trump. The two had a back-and-forth in April over Leo’s opposition to the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran, and Leo has also criticized the Trump administration’s migration crackdown. Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping last week in Washington, and while Xi said that it was important to ensure AI is “always under human control,” Trump focused more on trying to rebrand it as “superintelligence” and dismissed calls for regulation. However, the two leaders agreed to explore a new “notification mechanism” for AI incidents affecting national security. AI has become a major election-year issue in the U.S. as some of the country’s largest companies rush to build a national network of data centers while Americans from both parties increasingly raise alarms about the impact on farmland, water supplies and electricity bills. The pope says he’s optimistic about solutions Worries about AI are continuing to grow inside and outside the industry, and reports continue to emerge about increasingly powerful systems that solve problems beyond human capacity but could also go rogue and carry out other, more harmful tasks. The worries have grown so loud that the CEO of OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, said in an interview with Fortune that his company would wait until next year to start selling its stock to investors on Wall Street as it focuses on safety. Leo noted that ever since he published his encyclical in May, the Vatican has received comments from people interested in being part of a broader conversation about AI. A Vatican commission is working to promote dialogue, study and investigation “to find ways to make sure that AI does not get to a point of destroying humanity or removing humanity from the conversation,” he said. Leo said he was “relatively optimistic” that solutions could be found. “I think there are enough people seriously interested in that and willing to look at that outside of the questions once again of power, who gets there first,” he said.
