articles.title: Bodhana Sivanandan: Meet the 11-year-old Indian-origin British chess prodigy who became the youngest woman grandmaster in history
articles.summary: Most kids at 11 are probably trying to figure out how to keep track of their homework or negotiate with their parents about weekend plans.
articles.body: Most kids at 11 are probably trying to figure out how to keep track of their homework or negotiate with their parents about weekend plans. Bodhana Sivanandan has taken a wildly different path. She’s managed to carve her name into the chess history books by becoming the youngest woman ever to earn the Woman Grandmaster (WGM) title. And she didn’t pull this off quietly at a local tournament; she did it while playing for England at the 2026 Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan.This wasn’t a fluke or a one-time hot streak. Per the International Chess Federation, Bodhana earned her third and final WGM norm at the Olympiad, which made her eligible for the WGM title. She stands at just 11, shattering a decade-old record held by Russia's Kateryna Lagno, who managed the feat at 12 years and four months. Now, the world’s youngest Woman Grandmaster is not just one for the record books; this achievement is a stepping stone in a story that doesn’t show signs of slowing down.How a lockdown hobby led Bodhana to world recordsLet’s start at the beginning: Bodhana’s story has “pandemic twist” written all over it. She was born in London in 2015 to an Indian family rooted in Tamil Nadu. One day, during the chaos and boredom of lockdown, a family friend stopped by before heading back to India and handed her a chess set. That tiny act changed everything. What started as something to pass the time quickly turned into a passion, and then into something approaching genius.She didn’t just get good; she rocketed ahead. By the time she was seven, she swept all 24 games at the European Schools Championship. In 2023, she started to pop up on the radar, impressively holding her own against grandmasters, folks often two or three times her age with years more experience.Then 2024 arrived. England selected her for its women's team at the Chess Olympiad in Budapest. She was just nine and, according to English chess authorities, became the youngest person ever to represent England in any sport on an international level. There she was, sitting across from players who had been competing since before she was born, not just surviving, but fighting for points.By 2026, she walked back into the Olympiad as England’s top player: not just a young curiosity, but the leader of the team.Bodhana Sivanandan: A trailblazing OlympiadIn Samarkand, at the 2026 Chess Olympiad, Bodhana played all 11 rounds on the first board for England, racking up eight points. That run not only gave her the record, it also finalized her WGM title, confirmed by FIDE, which is chess’s international governing body.This isn’t a title handed out for being “talented for her age” or because she’s a pleasant chess ambassador. The WGM demands consistent, top-level performance and a 2300 international rating, which isn’t remotely easy to get. You have to prove yourself, norm after norm, against the best.Breaking new ground, again and againBy July of 2026, Bodhana had a new headline to her name. At the Dole Open in France, she knocked off Marc'Andria Maurizzi, the reigning French champion and a grandmaster with a hefty 2,628 rating. At just 11 years and four months, she became the youngest girl on record to take down a grandmaster rated above 2,600, toppling a record linked to none other than Judit Polgár, the greatest female chess player ever. She also picked up her first International Master (IM) norm there, another first for someone so young.Maybe most impressively, these weren’t just “women’s records”; she’s inching closer to titles that are open to all players, whether men or women. The IM path is open, and her recent results look like she’s charging right down it.Britain’s youngest women’s chess champion, and that’s just the startAugust 2026 brought yet another milestone: at the British Chess Championships in Coventry, she claimed the women's title, defeating Ireland’s Trisha Kanyamarala after a playoff. She’s already stacked up national championships in blitz and rapid and regularly faces, and sometimes defeats, older and more seasoned opposition.Look at her resume, and it’s almost like watching the records fall one after another: British champion, blitz champion, youngest on the Olympiad team, youngest WGM, and the list is still growing. Yet, you get the sense she isn’t obsessing over the numbers.When FIDE asked her what these milestones meant, she was clear: “I’m happy to do it, but I want to keep going and keep making history as well.” She’s more interested in the next move than the celebration.Still in primary school, but already a sporting legendIt’s hard to overstate what Bodhana has done. She started playing chess only a few years ago, for fun, at home, during a pandemic. Now, she’s an international champion, a record setter, and the youngest Woman Grandmaster in chess history. And all that before she’s even made the leap to secondary school.Bodhana’s story isn’t over, and honestly, it feels like it’s just opening its most exciting chapters!You use AI every day. articles.title: H1N1 dominates flu strains in India, accounts for 3 out of 4 cases: WHO
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: H1N1 is the dominant flu strain detected in India, accounting for three out of every four influenza-positive samples reported in the latest
articles.body: NEW DELHI: H1N1 is the dominant flu strain detected in India, accounting for three out of every four influenza-positive samples reported in the latest surveillance data, according to World Health Organization (WHO).The finding is from WHO's surveillance data for weeks 36 and 37 of 2026, covering Sept 1 to 14 and updated on Sept 21. Across the South-East Asia region, 817 of 3,632 samples tested positive for influenza, giving an overall positivity rate of 22%.India stood out for a high share of H1N1 among its positive samples. The A(H1N1)pdm09 accounted for 75% of influenza-positive samples in India, compared with 50% across the region. It was also the dominant strain in Bhutan and Thailand, where it accounted for 97% and74% respectively.Dr Rommel Tickoo, senior director, internal medicine, Max hospital, said H1N1 remains a seasonal strain, with higher complication risks for older adults, pregnant women, young children and people with underlying illnesses. He advised vaccination, respiratory hygiene, early testing where appropriate and timely antiviral treatment for high-risk patients.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Reparations activist does not expect compensation from New York officials as action is delayed for years
articles.summary: The U.S. Freedmen Project said New York's reparations commission delay proves the system is designed to stall, not deliver, for descendants.
articles.body: A reparations activist with a grassroots organization called the U.S. Freedmen Project told Fox News Digital that their group expects no financial compensation from New York state officials after lawmakers quietly delayed a high-profile study into historic remedies. "What the mainstream reparations movement is really about ... is spinning your wheels until [those] to whom the debt is owed tire out, give up, and give in," U.S. Freedmen Project President Devine Prince told Fox News Digital. "That's the only reason why you would pursue race-based policies within a system and within a country that has the 14th Amendment, which bans and prohibits race-based policies." The U.S. Freedmen Project — a group of self-identified "Foundational Black Americans" — aims to educate the public on the legal and historical distinctions between African Americans who are direct descendants of enslaved people in the U.S. and immigrants from Africa or the Caribbean who arrived voluntarily in recent decades. CHAOS ERUPTS AT NY REPARATIONS HEARING AS ‘FOUNDATIONAL’ BLACK AMERICANS CLASH WITH LEFT-LEANING GROUPS Prince’s comments follow sharp backlash after state leaders extended the timeline for the New York State Community Commission on Reparations Remedies to issue its final report. A provision embedded in the recently passed state budget pushed the commission's deadline back two years — from 2027 to 2029 — nearly four years beyond its original 2025 deadline. The New York Civil Liberties Union (NYCLU) publicly criticized the delay in June. "The state’s decision to spend an additional three years before it takes any action to address these harms raises a lot of questions about when Black New Yorkers will receive reparations," said Chantelle Williams, assistant director of the NYCLU’s Racial Justice Center. "Meanwhile, the impact of discrimination continues to harm Black individuals and communities across the state. This delay is not just a bureaucratic inconvenience. It is a disservice to those who have suffered the profound and lasting consequences of inequality," Williams added. NEW YORK FAR-LEFT GROUP CLAIMS REPARATIONS 'OWED' AS BLACKS' MEDIAN WEALTH 'NEARLY 15 TIMES LESS' THAN WHITES The nine-member state commission, established by legislation signed by Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul in late 2023, was tasked with examining the Empire State's historical ties to slavery, Jim Crow-era discrimination, and economic disparities like redlining. The panel was charged with delivering recommendations for potential state-level financial compensation and policy reforms. The commission recently concluded a series of statewide public hearings, culminating in a May 30 forum in Harlem titled "From Extraction to Repair: Closing the Racial Wealth Gap." However, state lawmakers opted to move back the commission's deadline. Assemblymember Michaelle C. Solages, D-N.Y., who sponsored the original legislation, acknowledged the extension was requested to navigate a shifting national legal environment. Solages cited conservative legal challenges targeting diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) initiatives and the broader erosion of race-conscious policies. The budget measure also included a provision shielding commissioners from personal legal liability if targeted by lawsuits over their findings. Lineage advocates with the U.S. Freedmen Project, who attended the Harlem hearing, pushed back strongly against both the delay and the commission's framework. They argue that reparations should be strictly limited to direct descendants of individuals enslaved within the United States rather than broader race-based categories. Activists with the group contend that progressive organizations like the NYCLU fail to represent the distinct legal and historical claims of descendant Black Americans by attempting to include recent Black immigrants under the same umbrella. Prince claimed that members of the New York commission were appointed to preserve the status quo rather than deliver tangible results. "These are individuals that have been put in place to keep the status quo intact while pretending they're working to undo it," Prince said. "There's a bunch of things moving around in the background that tie them to this ideology that benefits them if we keep the status quo of race-based advocacy alive." "What we are focused on is true repair — and, unfortunately, true repair means repairing those who were truly harmed. Not everyone who comes in and says, 'Hey, I'm included in that, too,'" he added. Supporters of the Freedmen Project maintain that any state-level reparations bill based on race rather than direct lineage would violate the U.S. Constitution's Equal Protection Clause. They urged state officials to adopt strict lineage-based criteria to reduce the program's exposure to legal challenges. New York is part of a broader wave of blue states and municipalities attempting to construct local reparative frameworks. In Illinois, the Chicago suburb of Evanston, Illinois made headlines as the first U.S. city to distribute reparations, offering $25,000 housing grants to eligible Black residents. Despite public hearings and ongoing research, Prince expressed skepticism that New York state will ever deliver payments to descendants. TRUMP ADMIN VOWS TO STOP REPARATIONS PROGRAMS, ACCUSES OFFICIALS OF 'VIRTUE SIGNALING' TO GET 'VOTES' "Realistically, I'm expecting the same thing that I expected going into this: nothing," Prince said. "Based on all the advocacy we did before this was even signed into law — all the recommendations we suggested and experts we brought to the New York Legislature to inform them on how to get this right — once all those things were ignored, I knew it would end up right where it is now. Realistically, I'm expecting them to find a way to distance themselves from this." articles.title: Evicted Spanish pensioner, Maricarmen Abascal, can move home, lawyer says
articles.summary: The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, 87, prompted large-scale protests across Spain.
articles.body:
An evicted elderly disabled woman, who became symbolic of Spain's housing crisis, will be able to return to her home in Madrid, according to her lawyer.

Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years on 23 September. She was admitted to hospital after the eviction.

The eviction led to widespread anger across Spain, and prime minister Pedro Sanchez has promised housing relief measures when his cabinet meets on Tuesday.

Abascal's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, told a press conference there had been "goodwill from both parties" and that she would pay a similar amount of rent under a new contract, averting a significant price hike.

Abascal's father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.

Investment firm Urbagestión, which bought the property in 2018, increased the rent from €500 per month (£428; $572) to €2,650 (£2,280; $3,020).

The company later offered to reduce this to €1,650 however she was still unable to pay this with her monthly pension of €1,350.

Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts.

Her case triggered nationwide protests and tens of thousands of people to march through the Spanish capital on Saturday to object to the eviction and to demand stronger protection for tenants in the face of a housing shortage and soaring rents.

Duro said the agreement, yet to be signed, was the "result of the social mobilisation".

She added that Abascal, who is being treated for exhaustion, would sign the deal when she feels better.

Supporters called it a victory but promised to continue their fight to prevent similar evictions, and to press for more affordable housing.

The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction.

Pedro Sanchez's Socialist Party, which lacks a majority in Parliament, is hoping to pass a law to appease public outrage.

articles.title: Why do hotel towels have those horizontal stripes near the edges? The real reason behind that familiar design.
articles.summary: Discover the real reasons behind the horizontal stripes on hotel towels. Learn how this design serves practical functions in construction, presentation, and durability while maintaining a clean aesthetic.
articles.body: Walk into almost any hotel bathroom and there is one small detail you are likely to notice on the towels. Whether they are fluffy white bath towels, hand towels or face towels, many of them have one or more horizontal stripes woven into them, usually close to the edges. At first, these stripes may look like nothing more than a decorative touch. After all, hotels are known for their neat, minimalist white linen, and the stripes add an extra texture without making the towel look colourful or flashy.But there is actually more to this than just aesthetics.These horizontal bands are often called dobby borders or dobby stripes, referring to the weaving technique used to create them. While the exact pattern can vary from manufacturer to manufacturer, and, hotel to hotel, the design has several practical purposes as well.It is not just decorationThe most obvious reason for the stripe is to give the otherwise plain towel some visual definition. Hotel towels are generally white because white linen gives a clean, uniform appearance and can be washed at high temperatures and treated with bleach when appropriate.A completely plain white towel, however, can look rather indistinguishable from another. The woven border creates a simple visual break and gives the towel a more finished appearance without compromising the clean look hotels prefer.Unlike printed designs, these stripes are woven into the fabric itself. This means there is no separate coloured layer sitting on top of the towel that could fade or peel away with repeated washing.The stripes also mark the construction of the towelMost towels are made from absorbent loops of yarn, commonly cotton, that form the familiar soft, fluffy surface. The area near the edge needs to be constructed differently because the towel has to be finished in a way that prevents the fabric from continuing to unravel.The woven border creates a denser, flatter section at the end of the towel. In other words, the stripe helps separate the main absorbent body of the towel from its finished edge.That does not mean the stripe alone is responsible for stopping a towel from fraying. The hem and the way the towel is woven and stitched are important too. But the border is part of the towel's overall construction and helps create a neat transition between the looped pile and the edge.Why is the stripe usually near the borders of the towel?The middle of a towel is where maximum absorbency and softness are needed. Putting a denser woven pattern through the centre would mean replacing some of those absorbent loops with a flatter weave.The border, on the other hand, is an area where absorbency is less important. Placing the tighter weave close to the edge therefore allows manufacturers to add structure and visual detailing without taking too much away from the towel's main purpose.This is also why you will often see the stripe running horizontally across the towel rather than covering a large portion of it.It can make folding and presentation easierHotels deal with enormous quantities of towels every day. A towel may be washed, dried, folded, stacked, transported and placed in a bathroom many times over its life.The border provides an easy visual reference when folding the towel. Housekeeping staff can use the woven band as a rough guide to create a consistent fold, helping stacks of towels look uniform.This is particularly useful in hotels where presentation matters. A pile of identically folded white towels gives a bathroom that crisp, organised appearance that is difficult to achieve when every towel is folded differently.Of course, modern housekeeping does not depend on the stripe to fold towels correctly. It is simply a convenient feature of a design that already serves other purposes.Are the stripes actually more hygienic?Not really. You may have come across claims that the horizontal stripe has some special hygienic function, but there is no general rule that the stripe itself makes a towel cleaner or more sanitary.The hygiene of a hotel towel depends much more on how it is washed, dried, stored and handled. The woven border is primarily a construction and design feature.So, if you have ever wondered whether the stripe is somehow a separate antibacterial section of the towel, the answer is no. It is not a secret hygiene technology hidden in your hotel bathroom.Why do luxury hotels specifically use them too?Interestingly, the design has survived even as hotel interiors have become more sophisticated.Luxury hotels often use extremely thick, high-quality towels, but the basic design remains remarkably familiar. That is because the border combines several things hotels value: a clean appearance, durability, easy presentation and a subtle decorative element.It also fits into the broader visual language of hospitality. White towels with a simple woven border look polished without appearing overly designed.The next time you pick up a hotel towel and notice those horizontal stripes, therefore, it is worth looking at them a little differently. They are not merely an attempt to make a plain towel look fancy. They are part of the way the towel is woven and finished, while also giving it a neat visual identity.And like many ordinary objects in a hotel room, that tiny detail is a reminder that even something as simple as a towel has been designed around appearance, function and the realities of being washed and used hundreds of times.You use AI every day. articles.title: Ancestral home of '62 war hero in Uttarakhand to be made museum
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Rifleman Jaswant Singh Rawat's inimitable bravery in the battle of Nuranang against the advancing Chinese troops in 1962 is an indelible part
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Rifleman Jaswant Singh Rawat's inimitable bravery in the battle of Nuranang against the advancing Chinese troops in 1962 is an indelible part of popular lore. A memorial to honour him was built by the Army at the site of his supreme sacrifice in the border region of Arunachal Pradesh.A biographical movie '72 Hours: Martyr Who Never Died' depicting his remarkable story as a soldier of the 4th battalion of Garhwal Rifles was made too. However, what remained missing was a befitting memorial to the Mahavir Chakra awardee at his ancestral village in Uttarakhand.BJP MP Anil Baluni, who represents Garhwal constituency in Lok Sabha, said the late soldier's home at Baryun village of Pauri Garhwal will be developed into a modern museum. He will perform 'bhoomi pujan' for the project on Nov 17.While the 'Jaswant Garh War Memorial' in Arunachal Pradesh is a draw for visitors and tourists, a museum at the place of his birth is expected to further cement his legacy in his home state, which sends men to the armed forces in large numbers when compared to its relatively small size.Baluni said he had met the martyred soldier's family members who consented to the initiative and appreciated the project. Rawat had enlisted in 4th Garhwal Rifles on Aug 19, 1960, at the young age of 19. He was just 21 when he laid down his life on Nov 17, 1962.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
